notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00538.opp-gr: §3: 'λοῦντος' is evidently defective; read as καλοῦντος ('calling down upon himself'). 'διατρῆσαι' taken as διατηρῆσαι ('preserve'). §11: 'ἴδει' read as ἔδει.

§29: the text near the end is corrupt: 'καὶ λέγ’ ὄντων καὶ]' cannot be construed (the edition's bracket appears unmatched); rendered as [...]. The following sentences ('And will you bear with the rich man?...') seem addressed to the wronged husband, but the connection is uncertain. §21: 'ἔξω βλέπεις' ('look abroad') presumably means looking toward the enemy. §26: 'ἀτίμους' of others' children presumably refers to bastards begotten in adultery losing civic rights.

§32: the herald's curse presumably refers to the formal curse on those who deceive the people/jury; 'these' (acquitted) are the deceived jurors, 'those' the deceivers. §33: <ἔμελλεν> is an editorial supplement. §39: 'for not myself at least' is awkward; Greek οὐ γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ γε, i.e. 'not, at any rate, myself'.

'RIV 568 |' is a page reference from the printed edition and has been left out. 'ἀπάξουσι ... ὡς ἐμέ' is taken as 'will lead you off to me', i.e. hand you over to the speaker. It could also be read as 'will lead you off, as [they would] me'.

nodes.text: XXXVIII.

There was a rumour that the rich man was sleeping with the poor man's wife. The poor man proposed a law ordering that adulterers be killed without trial. The rich man indicted it [as illegal]. He won, and the poor man now prosecutes him for adultery.
The Declamation.

If this man here, judges, had been willing for the law about adulterers that I recently proposed to come into force, we would not now be troubling you with indictments and accusations; rather, those wronged in respect of their wives would have been able to help themselves. But since the rich man, having prevented that, compels us to do this, I beg all of you to bear in mind that you too have wives, and to listen accordingly, and not to suffer the same as those who judged the case about the law, in which, though I spoke most justly and in the interest of the whole city, I came away defeated by this man and by his cleverness and preparation. The result was that he grew proud, while those who had voted were spoken ill of by some, on the grounds that they had valued the favour of the rich man more highly than themselves, their wives and their children.

Yet that business about the law seems not to have been altogether useless to me. For even if it could not come into force because of this man's ambitious rivalry in the contests, it at least taught me better about my own great misfortunes, and the speech he made against the law at that time has given no small proof for this present accusation. For he who alone of all the citizens feared that we who are wronged in respect of our wives might gain the power to kill those who wrong us, how did he not plainly admit that I had good reason to legislate in such a way, and that he himself had done something of the kind, and was daring it, and would not even stop?

3. It would therefore be a mark of great idleness and misfortune, when the adulterer is calling the prosecutor down upon himself, neither to answer the challenge nor to exact a penalty for his drunken outrage; and it would be fitting for you too to be angry and to achieve two things with one vote: to exact a penalty for what I have suffered, and to preserve the marriages of those who have not yet suffered the same as I. They will indeed gain more from the trial than I. For my misfortunes will remain even if this man dies ten thousand times, and no judge could undo any of them; but those who have not yet had experience of him in their own wives will be assured of never having it.

Now if what this man has done against us were unknown to the city, I might perhaps out of shame have hidden in silence an evil that was unknown; but since you have not stopped talking and hearing about these things for a long time now, there is no reason for me to hesitate to mention to you things of which I think not even the very young are unaware.

5. Above all, I think, this man will pay the penalty for refusing to behave himself, unless indeed he is so great that he alone of all men has been granted leave to commit adultery with whatever women he likes and to fear neither accuser nor proof; but even so, it is no small thing for me to lament my misfortunes before you. For to speak about themselves brings some consolation to those who have suffered the greatest wrongs.

6. Formerly, then, I supposed that the poor who chose to marry were sensible, since they would have some support from the wife herself, who shares the other labours and contributes the work of her hands, and more from the children as they come to manhood and support them in old age; but now those of the poor who do not shun marriage seem to me out of their minds, and much more so those who marry beautiful women, for they marry them not for themselves so much as for those able to corrupt them.

Something of this kind has happened in my case too. For since my wife had a share of beauty, judges, and was praised for it, and often went out of the house as constant necessity required, as is the way of wives in poverty, who reasonably perform for themselves the services of maidservants, this man saw her and at first, naturally, admired her, then addressed her, then, sending her love-messages and money and hopes for a long time, as I later learned, though failing to persuade her, at last he persuaded her. And she began to disdain me, was annoyed when I was present and glad when I went out, and was plainly looking wholly towards another man.

So this man, enjoying my wife, going in to her whenever it was safe, and taking her wherever he wished, having enslaved the soul of the wretched woman and finding her obedient in everything, could not, because of the constancy of his outrage and drunkenness, escape notice. And the city was full of this story. In the barber-shops and the perfume-shops and in the marketplace and in the houses this was the common talk: 'Adultery is being dared in the city; the one daring it is the rich man', naming this admirable fellow, 'and the one robbed of his wife is the poor man', adding my name.

But for a long time I went on knowing nothing. For none of my enemies was so cruel as to come up and reproach me, and my friends shrank from becoming messengers of such things. But as the rumour grew and the disgrace became extreme, my friends thought it terrible that I should never learn of it, and coming to me, looking at the ground, falling silent for some time and weeping, they said: 'Good friend, we ought to have better news to report to you, but since events do not allow it, we know that we shall grieve you by speaking; yet it is more the part of friends to speak than to keep silent.' And they told me just what I am now telling you.

How I was beside myself and how I collapsed on hearing it, little short of madness, those then present know; but when at last I had barely come to myself, I considered how I might either punish this man or make him better through fear, and on reflection I found that the man who first laid down the laws for the city had arranged other matters well, had honoured the virtues as he ought, and had dealt not badly with those who commit other wrongs, but had not imposed on these adulterers all that he should. If someone robs this man of money, he at once granted him the right to kill in self-defence, and the one who has done this is held to be free of guilt; but if someone robs a husband of his wife, 'Divorce her', he says, 'indict him, and pray to the gods to get a court', but he did not grant the right to kill.

Believing that this has caused many adulteries, I proposed a law, judges, which had been overlooked by those before, and which would force even the man not so disposed by nature to behave himself. Now the decent and moderate men, those stronger than shameful desires, admired it and praised it: 'This law', they said, 'should have been laid down long ago.' But this splendid and great man, who overruns the houses of the poor, knowing that the law would be laid down against himself first, was indignant, slandered it, trembled, hired orators, prevailed over justice with words, and having prevented the law from coming into force, he followed me about with his many flatterers, laughing at me, mocking me and calling me 'lawgiver'.

12. So, since everyone cries out that he convicts himself of adultery by his fine accusation, I have come to punish him with your help, if indeed I am able; but he says he is dreadfully treated if he is to be destroyed when no one testifies against him. For he thinks the whole city counts for nothing: popular leaders, orators, private citizens, so many tribes, citizens, resident aliens, foreigners, all of whom have condemned him in their souls, so that he goes about with his deeds known to people who know them exactly and do not keep silent. And you know, judges, it has often been said, and you have often heard it.

What greater testimony, then, could anyone present in a court than that even the judges, before entering, had condemned the defendant? So when, this being the case, he calls me a sycophant, he calls you so along with me, and all who inhabit the city, and together with all these the goddess too. For we have learned from the wisest poets that Rumour is a goddess.

And trusting her we consider some men better and others worse. And one man has been thought a traitor, another a murderer, another a tomb-robber, each one something or other of this kind, though those who say so have not seen these things being dared, but cannot disbelieve the rumour, which must take its origin from what has been done. And I see that cities derive the greatest benefits from this goddess, who does not let even things done in deep darkness go unnoticed, bringing everything into the light, handing it over to men and exposing those who contrive anything.

Fortune did not give me male and female servants, acting after her own fashion, for she allots different things to different people. So now I cannot call household slaves as witnesses, for how could I call those who do not exist? But I call on your voices and on what you have learned this man did to my wife, the unfortunate woman, who was brought down by his wealth.

Nor again can it be said that, however passionately he loved [her], he would not have been able to persuade her for lack of money. For who of you does not know his great wealth: the gold, the apartment blocks, the slaves, the herds, the land, the monthly interest? And a man who is both in love and rich would quickly win over a woman's mind. For nothing is so apt to rout chastity as the power to give lavishly. Even if she repels the first attempt, more gifts come, and then as many again, and the daily increase does not stop short of victory.

This, judges, is what makes traitors: the enemy buying their services at a high price. This persuades men to neglect their just duties to their country; this has brought about many adulteries. And the desire for more has before now dragged down even a woman living in abundance. And if even a rich woman has been dazzled by more, what wonder is it that the poor man's wife was somewhat affected by gold?

And I do not say this because I pardon her, for let nothing be more precious to a woman than her husband, but because it was to be expected that a woman of no means would be overwhelmed by the money sent to her, and, having received what she needed, would give in return what the giver wanted. I do not say this against every poor woman, for it is possible, it is possible for a woman to be poor and yet impregnable, but because, for a rich man who wishes to commit such wrongs, having great possessions can often help.

19. Now, though these too are no small proofs that this man has done what he is thought to have done, what I am about to say is much greater. For if this man were not an adulterer, judges, why was he fighting the law that guards marriages? Rather, if this man were not an adulterer, he would have proposed this law himself before me, contending against the rumour with it and making it plain to all: "I, the wicked man of ill repute who wrongs the married citizens, am the one who legislates such measures against adulterers." Who would not have praised him then, judges? Who would not have welcomed it? Who would not have cursed those who dared to speak against it? Who would not have admired the speech?

But he was so far from doing anything of the kind that he even regarded me, the lawgiver, as an enemy, shouting, threatening, gathering against the proposal those who do not use their speech well. So when you were doing this, you were then testifying that you commit adultery. For why should a man conscious of no such thing fear the punishment?

If I were proposing a law against temple-robbers and you were indignant, would that not be an admission that you had stolen the property of the gods? If against those who steal public funds and you were vexed, would you not be among the thieves? If against traitors and you opposed the law, would you not be making it plain that you look abroad [to the enemy]? So now too, by setting yourself against what is proposed against adulterers, do you not admit that it was proposed against you? It would be strange if making war on adulterers is a sign of chastity, while helping them will not seem proof of committing adultery.

22. Now I know that he will say the rumour is the work of envious men. For it is likely that the well-off are envied by the poor. For we must, it seems, judges, be insulted not only elsewhere but in the courts too. For what greater evil could anyone hear said of himself than that he is choking over other people's good fortune? But we ask the gods for blessings for ourselves and our children, and we have never judged the prosperity of others a misfortune of ours.

I would gladly ask you whether you alone of those in the city have great wealth. May we never fare so badly that only one house prospers in it. How then, most clever man, when you are well-off along with many, do you say that you alone are envied? For if this were so by nature, all the well-off would have to hear many terrible things from these people, if indeed being rich necessarily brings envy, and the envied are necessarily slandered in this way. But you see that we love the others and admire them and rejoice with them in their prosperity and join in praying that their property may increase, and we call them common parents of the people. And no one says any of them commits adultery. Why? Because none of them does commit adultery.

And you too, then, if you had chosen to be chaste, would have met with the same treatment. But as it is, not your wealth but your wrongdoing has produced this rumour; since, if it were hatred born of envy that surrounded you, and these things were said so that you might be ruined, other charges would be made, greater than these and far more terrible, able to turn the whole city into your enemy. What are these? They would accuse you of plotting revolution, of resenting equal freedom of speech, of claiming to be greater than the many, and of seeking to put yourself in place of the laws. And the story would not be unconvincing, since all who have ever overthrown democracies have done it with the help of wealth.

But as it is, you are telling me of great folly in the envious, if, wishing to harm you, they did not do it more forcefully. For then they would have set the whole city on you, whereas now they were not stirring up so many of the citizens against you. For fear of slavery and the outrage done to a woman are not equal in rousing anger. Why then do they leave that aside and say this? Because the one you have not yet conceived, but the other you have done. Then, as though you were afraid on behalf of those who call you an adulterer that they might seem to be lying, you came to accuse a law that does not permit adultery, showing that the law had produced results.

26. "And what law," he says, "was I breaking by accusing?" And what of it? Was I not allowed to accuse? Or am I one of the disenfranchised? You are not disenfranchised, though you would justly be, having made other men's children disenfranchised; nor again did you indict without having the right to do so, for you had it. But what is being judged today is not this, whether you indicted lawfully or not, but whether by indicting you did not bear witness against yourself. For it is also allowed to walk through the alleys and to look up as you walk; but if you often walk the same way with no necessity driving you, and often look up, eyeing a young and beautiful woman who is nothing to you, you are doing what is not forbidden by law, but by doing it you show for what purpose you do it.

So too now we do not seek punishment for the indictment, nor is that the charge; but we find the indictment a trustworthy sign of what we charge, and by abolishing the death that follows being caught in the act you have subjected yourself to the death that comes from the vote. For you could no longer deny what you have admitted. For finding fault with the law contains the admission of adultery.

28. "But I did not indict for this reason," he says, "but because I saw that he was proposing what was neither just nor expedient." How not just, by Zeus? Is it not just that the woman a man has married should be his? Is it not just that legitimate children be born to the city? And why is it not also expedient that fathers should have offspring free of suspicion? At any rate, in this way they would also serve in war with greater goodwill.

"But killing a man untried is not just." And what need is there of a trial when I catch you in my own bed? What need is there, when the crime is plain, to obtain a suit? If the man who has entered another's house, entwined himself with another's wife and lain with her in the husband's place, is not slaughtered at once on the bed in which he committed this outrage, but is summoned to court and enters having rehearsed the laws and brings in people to plead for him, and the man who has suffered such things, though a sword is at hand and so bitter an intercourse is seen, puts up with it and escorts the adulterer to the door like a benefactor, is this, rich man, just? Is it not just to use a noble anger for killing, but [only] to put up the next day with those who console and frighten and [...] And will you bear with the rich man? For will you not go away having gained another evil besides?

30. "How then," you will say, "if this was just, was it not in the old laws?" But how many other things that are just nowadays were not in the old laws, things which time found as it went on! Do you not see laws, practically every month, some being repealed and others being proposed, as circumstances themselves suggest such things, that it is better for this rather than that to prevail? For even if those who laid down the laws long ago were quite wonderful in their nature, they were at any rate human, and it is no wonder that something needful escaped a human mind.

So the law was better than the [old] law, and for this reason it pleased all the rest, but it grieved you alone, and for this reason you were indignant. And yet if it were bad it would have had everyone indignant. But they do not suffer from your disease. That is why they were not afraid either. So one would sooner take the silence of the others as a sign that the law is beneficial than this man's fear as a sign that it is not expedient.

"And yet I was winning," he says. But wrongly. And how many rich men before you have won wrongly! Did the jurors, then, act impiously? No, by Zeus, but they were deceived. And it is not the same thing to give up justice willingly and to be misled. For the one belongs to the wickedness of the man who does a favour, the other to the craft of those who distort the truth. And no one would blame the one who suffered instead of the one who acted. For the herald too, while he acquits these, curses those. So do not slander me before those jurors who, along with me, have been wronged by your power, which you have used in full measure everywhere, in the marketplace, in the council chamber, in the assemblies, in the law courts. So you prevailed unjustly, but you feared a law that was good and that helped married men, and by your fear you admitted to committing adultery.

33. "Perhaps I feared the suspicion arising from the indictment," he says. But the fear was greater in not indicting. For the one involved death, the other a trial. And against the latter he <was likely> not to be at a loss for arguments, but against the former he would have nothing. So he thought a fight against evidence safer than a fight against the sword.

34. Apart from this, men also do many things through the anger of the gods, by which they show themselves up as their own accusers and draw their judges to them by the holds they offer. And now those [gods], making the proofs of this man's wickedness more numerous, have added second signs to the first.

And what if he knew he could easily bear the disgrace arising from suspicion, having lived in it for a long time already, but did not think there would be anyone to try him, because of his wealth and his arrogance and his choregic sponsorships, trumpeted everywhere? For the same reason, then, he prosecuted in person, and did not do it through another. For he would not have persuaded any of the best men, and a flatterer would not have been able to bring in, among the arguments about the law, his own and his ancestors' public services.

36. "And how much better," he says, "to have hunted him down and dragged him in, rather than to prosecute on the basis of signs." Because it is hard for a poor man to put aside his worries about his livelihood and sit keeping watch for an adulterer. Next, I think I would have endured anything to kill him once caught; but if even then I was going to bring him to trial, why should I not do so now? What weakness have I found in the evidence? Do we not know of countless men convicted by such evidence? So let him too pay the penalty, refuted by many and very clear [proofs].

You will vote today, jurors, about things you know. What he has done you have often said and often heard. About these things you have sworn to those who disbelieved. When you saw this man you were indignant, and when he approached you fled. Often you called this man by his deed rather than by the name his father gave him. And anyone who said "the adulterer" would at once have indicated this man.

And you blamed me for being insensible of my own misfortune: "Has this wretch no ears? No eyes? No relatives? No friends? Does he know nothing? Has he heard nothing? When will he go into court and teach the rich man that the fruits of this pleasure are bitter?" And when I belatedly realised that I no longer had my wife, many married men came to me and begged me to cut out this destroyer, "and grant us," they said, "to feel confident about our wives."

39. So I have come to do this and to help you, for not myself at least. For my case is incurable, but the gain would be yours, who do not yet lament such things. So it is right that the zeal be common to all, but especially the poor should care about what this man has learned to despise and against which [he has learned] to use his practice. For if, heaven forbid, he should be acquitted and you should grant him this, who will he be once he has gained licence, he who did such things while the vote held him in fear?

I am not the only one, jurors, who has a beautiful wife, but perhaps some of you have too. This man knows exactly how many; I suppose some. So fear, as many of you as have one; or rather, simply all of you who have wives, fear. For I hear that for those who are drawn to this, adultery itself brings delight, even if there is no beauty to enjoy.

41. But even if one of the gods guaranteed to you, jurors, that this man would not lay hands on your households, would you not reasonably pity me even so, who both have children and have none? For sometimes they seem to be mine, sometimes not mine. And I sit deliberating: shall I throw them out of the house as not mine? Or shall I raise them and consider them my own seed?

And even if this is truly so, for let us suppose it, jurors, who will rescue them from reproaches? Who will tolerate them taking part in public life with freedom of speech? Who will not muzzle them? Who will not drag them from the speakers' platform? That men who do not even know whom they were born from should dare to speak and address the people? Must they not then cover their heads and run away?

And why do I speak of the children? Have I not lost my voice too? For if I ever came forward and said something expedient for the city but painful to some, at once someone will stand up and say: "A fine guardian of our constitution this man will be, as [he was] of his own house!" And will my wife's kin have a share in any better position? How could they?

44. You see how many people one man has drenched in disgrace. Why, noble and rich sir? For what wrong did you exact this penalty? Did I take gold from you? Or silver? Or clothing? Or did I buy a plot near your estates and cut off some of your land? You could name none of these things, since they were not done.

Why then have you stolen and hold the one possession I had (for a wife is a poor man's only possession)? Did you desire beauty? Then was it not to be found among the courtesans? But, I suppose, in using them you would have outraged no one, wronged no one, made no one wretched, and your pleasure was in being able to do these things. That is why you passed them over and attacked me. Will you then not condemn this man who indulges in such luxuries, but put up with him talking of choregic sponsorships and trierarchies and how we poor are nowhere?

But it is not right, jurors, to demand such rewards for such expenditures. For it is neither lawful nor tolerable. Let it suffice for them, if they do these things well and eagerly, to be praised, and let no one seek licence for adultery in a democratic city. For if we will not grant this even to those who distinguish themselves in war, through whom the city has its safety, how should those who contribute a little out of much receive it?

We admit that we do nothing for our homeland with money, for we have none, and Fortune did not make us among the well-off; but what could come from men loyal and eager towards you has all been fulfilled, and you could not prove us bad or slow in such contributions.

48. I am amazed that you do not even feel shame before these men whom you have brought in to plead for you, who, having spent no less than you on these things and able to cite many voluntary donations and many public services of their own, nevertheless know how to be self-controlled; since even now they seem to me to have come here unwillingly, having condemned what this man has dared and knowing that because of him being wealthy has fallen into disrepute, but compelled by his many entreaties and his tears. May many blessings come to them, since they use well what they have.

49. But you are not such a man, you who are rich at the expense of the poor; you think that what is allowed to tyrants should be allowed to you while the laws still stand. But these men will lead you off to me today, and in this you would not prove more powerful than the courts. And once you are dead, perhaps the law too may come to be established, freed from your domination.
